DE-2025-HB122.s: This act changes how Family Court handles some criminal cases in Delaware. It removes a residency rule in the definition of "family" and lets Family Court and the Court of Common Pleas share authority over certain cases, including some where a child’s parentage is in dispute. It also covers some adult non-felony cases that fit both courts’ roles. The bill became law.

DE-2025-HB133.s: The law lets Delaware courts waive some fines and fees, in whole or in part, when a person cannot afford to pay. It creates a presumption that these charges will not be imposed in some cases, such as when a person gets public aid like Medicaid, SNAP, or veterans’ benefits, or is represented by the Office of Defense Services. It also sets up a hearing process for people who were already ordered to pay fines or fees, and it takes effect 180 days after enactment.

DE-2025-HB145.s: This law limits police and courts from using reverse location and reverse keyword searches, which are searches that look for people by where they were or by search terms they used. It generally bars requests and court orders for these searches, but allows reverse keyword searches in suspected Class A felony cases if the search returns 5 or fewer hits. It also says evidence from an illegal reverse keyword search must be kept out of court.

DE-2025-HB150.s: This law limits civil arrests in courthouses and in Department of Labor offices where the Delaware Industrial Accident Board holds hearings. A civil arrest can still happen there if a judge allows it or if law enforcement gives the court or agency detailed advance notice. It became law in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB188.s: The bill would let Delaware voters who are not part of a political party vote in that party's primary election. It would affect unaffiliated voters in Delaware. People who belong to a political party would still not be able to vote in another party's primary.

DE-2025-HB218.s: This law makes courts treat a military protective order as a reason to grant an emergency protective order or a temporary sexual violence protective order. It also requires police to tell the agency that issued a military protective order if they have probable cause to think a person broke that order. It affects people involved in military protective orders and sexual violence protection cases in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB219.s: The law makes Diwali Day a ceremonial day in Delaware and says it should be marked each year. It became law after passing the House and Senate and being signed by the governor.

DE-2025-HB222.s: The law updates the fine amounts for breaking Delaware's nutrient management rules. The State Nutrient Management Commission may now set a fine from $125 to $5,000 for each violation, instead of $25 to $1,000. It affects people and businesses covered by the state nutrient management program.

DE-2025-HB253.s: This law lets a person with a felony get permission to handle an estate if the Register of Wills agrees and there is good cause. Letters testamentary or of administration are papers that let someone manage a dead person's estate. It applies to people seeking to serve in that role in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB276.s: The law lets thefts that happened at different times be added together and charged as one case if they were part of the same course of conduct, meaning the same pattern of acts. It also defines that term and makes technical fixes to match state drafting rules. This affects theft cases in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB295.s: The law requires certain state buildings to have one or more reserved parking spaces for a veteran, set by the Director of the Office of Management and Budget. It also bans stopping, standing, or parking in that space, and these violations are not subject to the usual civil parking fine. It took effect 6 months after becoming law and also includes technical updates to Delaware law.

DE-2025-HB299.s: The law shortens the time a life insurance policy can limit coverage for death by suicide from 2 years to 1 year after the policy is issued. It applies to policies issued after the law takes effect, which is 6 months after it became law. If a death benefit is denied for suicide within that 1-year period, the insurer must refund all premiums paid for that coverage.

DE-2025-HB324.s: The law requires tattoo shops to post signs that raise awareness about human trafficking. It also directs the state health department to encourage tattoo shops and body piercing businesses to have workers learn how to spot, respond to, and report signs of human trafficking, and to refer people to victim help. The department must also make a free list of nonprofit groups that offer this training. It takes effect 1 year after becoming law.

DE-2025-HB326.s: This law raises the penalty for theft done by pretending to be the victim’s family member. A person convicted under this rule must serve at least 60 days in jail, and that minimum time cannot be suspended. It applies to people who commit this kind of theft in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB327.s: This law sets statewide rules for levels of newborn care at hospitals and other facilities with neonatal nurseries or neonatal intensive care units. It requires these facilities to meet national standards from the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the health secretary will assign each facility’s care level based on things like staff, equipment, and care rules. It also adds extra rules for Level IV NICU units, which care for the sickest newborns.

DE-2025-HB329.s: The bill would set time limits on a governor’s emergency order in Delaware. It would allow an emergency to last 120 days and be renewed for up to 60 more days, then let the General Assembly act on any longer extension. It would also require a report to the General Assembly every 30 days while a state of emergency continues.

DE-2025-HB337.s: Delaware law now requires folic acid to be added to corn masa flour and wet corn masa sold or used in the state. The products must meet set folic acid levels and show that folic acid on the nutrition label. The rule applies to corn masa foods, which are used in many diets.

DE-2025-HB341.s: The law changes child support rules for children committed to the Delaware Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families, or admitted to one of its services. It creates a rule that parents are generally not responsible for care and support in those cases. Family Court may order child support only if it would not block the parent and child from being reunited.

DE-2025-HB342.s: The bill would extend Delaware's ban on buying or having deadly weapons to people covered by protective orders from other states, not just Delaware Family Court orders. It affects people subject to those orders and those who sell or transfer deadly weapons.

DE-2025-HB356.s: This law limits the sale of class B firefighting foam with added PFAS chemicals starting January 1, 2028, with a longer exemption for some bulk petroleum facilities. It also requires notice for firefighting gear that contains PFAS and sets recall, reporting, and penalty rules for manufacturers and sellers. The law became effective when signed, and it affects foam and protective equipment makers, sellers, and some fuel facilities.

DE-2025-HB357.s: Delaware changed a state law to replace the term "poor person" with "a person unable to financially support oneself." It also makes clear that the duty to provide support can include an adult child with a disability who cannot support themself. The law became effective when it was signed by the governor.

DE-2025-HB363.s: This law lowers the speed limit in residential areas to 20 miles per hour. It gives 5 years to update road signs.

DE-2025-HB365.s: This act creates a Delaware Commission on Indigenous Affairs. The commission would work to advance and protect the interests of Indigenous people in Delaware. It passed both chambers and was signed by the governor, so it became law.

DE-2025-HB368.s: This law sets limits on when law enforcement and the Department of Correction can hold someone for immigration reasons. It bars detention based only on an immigration detainer or civil immigration warrant, with set exceptions for some people with violent felony, sex offense, DUI, or domestic violence convictions. It also restricts other help with civil immigration enforcement, requires some agency reports, and gives the Attorney General enforcement power.

DE-2025-HB371.s: This act removes the rule that each county must set up a Farmland Preservation Advisory Board. It also makes small wording fixes so the law matches Delaware's drafting standards. It became law in Delaware.

DE-2025-HB376.s: The law changes the Town of Millville charter by removing parts that already match state law and making other technical updates. It also updates the town’s election rules to add a final way to break a tie. The law removes a town-only property assessment process and sets a property tax cap at 3% of the town’s total assessed value.

DE-2025-HB380.s: This law updates Delaware’s personal data privacy rules to better match similar laws in other states. It lowers the size cutoff so the rules apply to businesses that handle personal data for at least 15,000 people, and it changes some rules for financial data and banks, insurers, and related companies. It also adds contract and check-up steps when businesses share personal data with third parties and makes other consumer privacy rules more alike across states.

DE-2025-HB381.s: This law changes Delaware rules on computer security breaches. It clarifies when businesses must tell the Attorney General after a data breach. It applies to businesses covered by the state law on breach notices.

DE-2025-HB384.s: The act lets Delaware use open-end contracts for highway building or rebuilding for up to five years. It applies to state highway construction and reconstruction contracts and keeps security in place to cover bids and work in progress. The law was signed by the governor and became Chapter 489.

DE-2025-HB388.s: The law changes how people handle a driver’s license when a medical condition stops them from driving. A person can keep the physical license for ID if they sign a statement saying they cannot drive. It also changes related state law and removes the need for some people to buy a separate ID card.

DE-2025-HB390.s: Delaware passed a law about how state agencies can take bids and hold bid openings. Agencies may use electronic bidding only, choose their own online platform, post results in real time and on their website within 2 business days, and skip a newspaper ad if they use the state electronic ad system. It also lets the agency and winning bidder agree to extend the time for a contract award, and it adds some rules for paper bids on certain smaller jobs.

DE-2025-HB393.s: The bill would add new rules for electric suppliers and their agents in Delaware. It would require training on sales and consumer protection, monthly reports on rates and customer choice, and written notices to customers before contract renewals or rate changes. It would also bar a single electric supplier agent from being fined or jailed for certain violations, and the bill was passed by the Senate before being vetoed by the governor.

DE-2025-HB404.s: The bill would create a 3-year pilot program in Delaware public schools to use artificial intelligence and extended reality, such as virtual reality and augmented reality, to support teaching and learning. The state Department of Education would run the program, help pay for the tools, and give technical help to up to 12 schools, including elementary, middle, and high schools in each county and in Wilmington. Participating schools would share data on how the program works, and the department would later send a report with its findings and advice on whether to expand or change it.

DE-2025-HB408.s: The law updates Delaware’s rules on trafficking and sexual servitude to match the federal standard for child sex trafficking. It makes it an offense to obtain or buy a minor for commercial sex, even if no third person like a pimp is involved. The change affects minors who are being exploited and can help them get state and federal support.

DE-2025-HB409.s: This law expands the crime of promoting prostitution in the second degree to cover people who knowingly run, manage, or advertise prostitution businesses. It also defines an "illicit massage establishment" as a place that uses a massage business as a cover for prostitution, and it makes that crime apply to people who control or operate those places. The law also makes related code updates and technical fixes.

DE-2025-HB411.s: This law renames the Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Enforcement to the Division of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Marijuana Enforcement. It also updates the state code to use the word “officers” instead of “agents” for people in the division. It became law in Delaware as Chapter 518 of Volume 85.

DE-2025-HB413.s: This law expands the use of revolving or flashing green lights to include vehicles and equipment used for road construction and maintenance. It affects workers and crews using those vehicles or equipment in Delaware. The measure was signed by the governor and became law.

DE-2025-HB414.s: Delaware changed the rules for cases about possessing a destructive weapon. It says adult cases go to Superior Court, while cases involving minors stay in Family Court.

DE-2025-HB418.s: The law updates Delaware’s rules on unmarked firearms, often called ghost guns. It gives people who already had these firearms before the law took effect a way to comply by having them marked with a serial number through a federally licensed dealer or by making them permanently unusable. It also updates some definitions and matches the state rules to federal serial number standards, while keeping the ban on untraceable firearms.

DE-2025-HB425.s: The law raises the salary supplement for school counselors and school nurses with national certification from 6% to 12%. It also adds school social workers to the group that can get the 12% supplement and says the payment applies only when the employee works in that profession. The Department of Education may also set rules to add other jobs that can get a salary supplement.

DE-2025-HB437.s: This act makes a set of technical fixes to Delaware law and to the town charters of Dewey Beach, Harrington, Houston, Milford, and Millsboro. It corrects wording, grammar, cross-references, and missing text in many parts of the state code, including rules on marijuana licenses, criminal law, schools, and health. The changes became law as Chapter 548.

DE-2025-HB439.s: This law sets rules for the sale of electric mopeds and electric motorcycles in Delaware. Sellers must give buyers a clear written notice about the vehicle’s legal class, power, and whether it needs registration, a license, and insurance. It also bars sellers from using terms like "electric bicycle" or "e-bike" for these vehicles and says mopeds may not be used on public pathways, bike lanes, or sidewalks.

DE-2025-HB446.s: The act updates Delaware’s agriculture and state forestry laws with technical wording changes to match state drafting rules. It adds plain definitions for "urban forestry," "urban forest," and "Urban Tree Canopy," and moves one section to a new spot in the code. It became law.

DE-2025-HB447.s: This law tells a state committee to help plan, develop, and fund child care affordability efforts. It allows the state to work with employers, community sponsors, and families on shared cost programs to expand access to licensed child care. It affects child care providers, families, employers, and state agencies.

DE-2025-HB449.s: This act would update Delaware’s rules for dietitians and nutritionists and split the current license into two types: licensed dietitian and licensed nutritionist. It would set different education, training, exam, and practice rules for each group, change board membership, and add a way to get a provisional license while waiting to pass the exam. It would also let current licensed dietitian/nutritionists move into one of the two new license types based on whether they hold the registered dietitian credential.

DE-2025-HB456.s: This law changes Delaware rules for permits on underwater state lands. It would make some permits easier to get, add some permit exemptions for work already approved by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and set faster review steps for minor projects. It also creates a Marine Contractors and Consultants Licensing Board to help DNREC with licensing and rules for people and businesses that affect submerged lands or tidelands.

DE-2025-HB459.s: The law bans selling energy drinks on public middle and high school campuses during school hours or school events. It affects schools, students, and anyone selling drinks on those campuses.

DE-2025-HB465.s: Delaware’s law adds virtual currency, like cryptocurrency, to the state’s money laundering rules. It also lets the state try to return virtual currency to crime victims, and if it cannot be returned, a court can decide how it is handled. The bill became law.

DE-2025-HB476.s: The law changes the Frederica town charter. It requires the town council to hold at least one regular meeting each month, instead of two set meetings on the first and third Wednesday. It also says that a new town ordinance takes effect right away unless the ordinance sets a different date.

DE-2025-HB63.s: This law changes Delaware’s fireworks rules by adding a permit system for fireworks sellers, raising fines, and requiring safety information for buyers. It affects fireworks retailers and people who buy or use fireworks in the state. It also gives the State Fire Marshal more oversight of fireworks sales and helps fund public education and enforcement.

DE-2025-HB84.s: Delaware’s law bars employers from requiring meetings or messages meant to share the employer’s political or religious views, including views about union organizing. It also sets out several exceptions, such as required legal notices, job-related information, and some communications by religious groups, political groups, schools, public employers, and certain tax-exempt groups. The state labor department can investigate, make rules, and bring court cases if needed, and it must update employer notice forms within 90 days of the law’s effective date.

DE-2025-HB89.s: The law creates a state help process for home improvement disputes between buyers and contractors. A buyer must first ask the contractor in writing to fix the problem and wait 20 days before asking for help from the Division of Consumer Protection. Contractors must take part in good faith, and buyers may be able to get damages, court costs, and lawyer fees if they sue under the consumer fraud law.

DE-2025-HB94.s: This law limits when state and local police can work with federal agents on civil immigration enforcement at child-serving places, colleges, houses of worship, and health care sites. They may do so only in urgent situations. If that happens, officers must file a report within 48 hours, and the reports are grouped into a twice-yearly report for lawmakers.

DE-2025-SB120.s: The law requires certain health plans to cover biomarker testing when there is medical and scientific support for the test. It applies to individual, group, state employee, and public assistance plans issued, renewed, changed, or reissued after December 31, 2027. It also says the coverage rule does not stop plans from using approved providers, using claim review rules, or covering screening, experimental, or investigatory biomarker tests.

DE-2025-SB189.s: This law changes Delaware insurance rules for settlements in personal injury cases from motor vehicle accidents. If a person was not represented by a lawyer when they agreed to a settlement, they must be given notice of a 15-day right to take it back if the payment is returned. It took effect 6 months after it was signed.

DE-2025-SB22.s: Delaware’s new law changes insurance rules for mental health and substance use disorder care. It requires private health plans to cover medically necessary treatment, including emergency care and certain out-of-network care when in-network options are not available, and it makes at least one form of some FDA-approved substance use disorder medicines go on the lowest-cost drug tier. It applies to individual, group, and blanket health plans issued or changed after December 31, 2027, and it also lets people ask for the plan’s mental health parity review, which is the check that coverage rules are fair compared with other care.

DE-2025-SB231.s: The bill would give a salary supplement to school social workers who pass the national clinical exam and hold a Licensed Clinical Social Worker license. It also makes small wording fixes to match Delaware's drafting rules. The measure passed the House but was later vetoed by the Governor.

DE-2025-SB232.s: This law makes criminal mischief a class F felony when someone intentionally damages an authorized emergency vehicle and causes at least $5,000 in loss or makes the vehicle temporarily unable to answer emergencies. It also makes technical wording fixes to match Delaware drafting rules. The change affects people charged with criminal mischief and emergency vehicles.

DE-2025-SB233.s: The law requires drivers to remove snow and ice from a vehicle before driving it. It adds a civil penalty, which is a money fine, for not doing so. It also sets a civil penalty when snow or ice falls from a moving vehicle and causes property damage or injury.

DE-2025-SB240.s: The law raises the highest draft limit for sixth class pilots from 27 feet to 29 feet. It affects pilot licenses in Delaware and is meant to cover deeper-draft ships. It also makes a few technical wording fixes to match state drafting rules.

DE-2025-SB249.s: This law sets rules for substance use harm reduction programs and gives immunity to program providers and staff. It also changes the rules for drug paraphernalia by decriminalizing possession for people who use drugs, while still keeping bans on items used to make or sell drugs. It also makes technical updates to match Delaware’s drafting rules.

DE-2025-SB257.s: Delaware now requires animal shelters in the state to get a license from the Department of Health and Social Services and renew it each year. First-time applicants must pass an inspection, and the department can deny, suspend, or revoke a license for rule breaks, false records, missed fees, or other listed problems. Shelters that operate without a license can get a warning or a civil fine of up to $1,000 for each violation. The law takes effect January 1, 2027.

DE-2025-SB27.s: The law creates an Office of New Americans in Delaware. The office is meant to help new Americans who come to the state and to support Delawareans overall. It became law on September 30, 2026.

DE-2025-SB271.s: The law changes how pharmacy benefits managers work with pharmacies and pharmacists in Delaware. It adds rules for audits, contract changes, appeals, rebate reports, and limits on sharing patient or prescriber information. It also sets notice rules, limits certain pricing and drug-dispensing practices, and says audit costs must be paid by the pharmacy benefits manager.

DE-2025-SB274.s: The law changes Delaware Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment forms to Delaware Portable Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment, or POLST forms, and keeps older DMOST forms valid. It also updates who can fill out these forms, who can decide if a patient cannot make that choice, and when that finding must be written in the medical record. The changes apply to patients with serious illness or frailty and to health care workers who complete these forms.

DE-2025-SB279.s: Would set a standard pay step for school-based occupational therapists in Delaware schools. It would help place them on the salary schedule more evenly, since training programs and college credit systems can differ. The change is meant to be similar to the way other school clinicians are paid.

DE-2025-SB280.s: The law adds rules for gift card theft and says a person can commit that crime by taking, changing, or using a gift card or its code without permission, with intent to cheat someone. It applies to people and businesses involved with gift cards, such as card holders, card issuers, and sellers. Gift card theft is punished under Delaware law's theft penalties, and the act became law.

DE-2025-SB281.s: This law updates state rules for the Delaware Hospital for the Chronically Ill, a long-term care facility in Smyrna. It removes outdated language and brings the rules in line with current care and admission practices. It also renames the facility the Eleanor Cain Center.

DE-2025-SB292.s: The law changes Delaware’s landlord-tenant rules for some housing providers and tenants. If part of a tenant’s rent is paid from a state reentry fund, the landlord must help make a discharge plan before ending the lease and give the required notice. It also tightens the rules for some housing operators that try to avoid eviction steps under the landlord-tenant code.

DE-2025-SB300.s: Delaware changed its rules for firearm dealers, who must now get a state license to sell or transfer firearms. The law sets rules for who can get a license, adds security, recordkeeping, training, background checks, and regular inspections, and allows fines or license loss for violations. It also sets license fees of $300 for an initial license and $250 to renew, and the changes begin to phase in by July 1, 2028.

DE-2025-SB305.s: The law creates a special Delaware State University license plate. Money from it would help student access, academic excellence, and university programs that support the school’s mission. It became law on September 14, 2026.

DE-2025-SB309.s: This act became law and stops the Department of Corrections from taking part of an inmate’s pay to cover a share of the cost of being housed in a facility. It also makes small wording fixes to match Delaware’s drafting rules.

DE-2025-SB318.s: This law ends the Delaware State Education Association centennial special license plate and replaces it with an updated version. The new plate is available to the public, and the plate number or letters will match the vehicle's current plate. Old centennial plates that were already valid stay valid.

DE-2025-SB319.s: This law requires health plans, the state employee plan, and Medicaid to cover needed tests and treatment for menopause and perimenopause, including hormone and non-hormone medicines, counseling, pelvic floor physical therapy, and bone health care. It also says insurers must give clear information about these benefits, and it limits some coverage rules for medically necessary hormone therapy. A religious employer with a group or blanket plan may ask for an exclusion if the coverage conflicts with its religious beliefs. It applies to policies changed or renewed after December 31, 2027.

DE-2025-SB324.s: The law gives a background-check exception for a qualified constable agency representative when buying handguns for constables to use on the job. It also lets the State Bureau of Identification void a purchase permit and revoke it if the person is no longer a qualified constable agency representative. The bill became law in Delaware as Chapter 497 of Volume 85.

DE-2025-SB325.s: The law updates fire prevention rules in Delaware and defines some terms in state code for clarity. It lets the State Fire Prevention Commission review criminal history records of fire company applicants and members to see if they are barred from serving because of certain crimes, including some felonies, sex crimes, drug crimes, and some financial or property crimes. It also updates the record-check language to match federal FBI request rules and makes technical fixes to the law.

DE-2025-SB330.s: Creates the Delaware African American Heritage and Culture Commission. The commission would serve as a statewide resource to help preserve and share Delaware’s African American culture and heritage. It was signed by the governor and became law.

DE-2025-SB332.s: The law says special vanity license plates in Delaware can be transferred from one owner to another. It applies to these personal property plates and clarifies that the transfer does not break a federal court order that blocks new special vanity plates or taking back ones already issued. It became law.

DE-2025-SB340.s: Long-term care facilities would have to carry insurance with at least $1 million per claim and $3 million total coverage for both general liability and professional liability. Professional liability is insurance for claims tied to care or services given by staff. The measure became law and took effect 180 days after it was signed.

DE-2025-SB345.s: The law changes Delaware criminal code language about minors and prostitution, using the words "exploited" and "exploitation" instead. It defines that term to mean acts by a minor that would count as prostitution if the person were 18 or older. It also updates related cross-references and adds a definition for "illicit massage establishment" if another bill becomes law.

DE-2025-SB349.s: The act names the Millsboro Bypass the "Senator Richard S. Cordrey Bypass." It applies to that highway name in Delaware. The measure became law.

DE-2025-SB355.s: This bill would change Delaware’s Freedom of Information Act, which is the law that lets people ask for public records. It would let anyone, not just state residents, make requests, require public bodies to answer in 10 business days, and let them charge some fees for scanning and reviewing records. It would also add new rules for when a request can be denied and update some record access rules for public colleges and universities.

DE-2025-SB361.s: This bill would change the State Employee Benefits Committee into the State Employee Benefits Council and add three working committees to help manage health care coverage for state workers and eligible pensioners. The new groups would handle health plan reviews, policy and planning, and financial review, and they would have powers to set quality measures, request audits, and get certain cost records from pharmacy benefit managers. It also would end one retiree health advisory subcommittee and take effect on January 1, 2028.

DE-2025-SB362.s: This bill would create a statewide registry for Parkinson’s disease and Parkinsonisms, overseen by the Department of Health and Social Services and run with help from the University of Delaware and the Delaware Health Information Network. Doctors, health care facilities, and clinical labs would have to report cases within 180 days of first diagnosis or treatment. The bill also sets data privacy rules, allows de-identified data to be used for approved research, requires a yearly report to the General Assembly starting January 1, 2029, and sets a $100-a-day fine for repeated noncompliance.

DE-2025-SB53.s: This act makes the Delaware Farm to Community Program part of state law. The program helps local farmers sell food to community groups that then give it to people in need across Delaware. It became law as Volume 85, Chapter 513.

DE-2025-SB94.s: The law updates the rules for respiratory care practitioners in Delaware. It lets qualified licensed respiratory therapists do all parts of extracorporeal life support, including giving medicine during the process, when they are trained to do so. It also makes technical fixes to match state drafting rules.

DE-2025-SJR21.s: This resolution directs the Department of Safety and Homeland Security to study whether it is practical to automatically store biological evidence. It affects that department and the handling of biological evidence, and it was signed by the Governor.
